title: Local-improvement procedures get stuck when satisfying discrete constraints

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Local-improvement procedures get stuck when satisfying discrete constraints

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: For discrete constraint systems the landscape of constraint violations is almost always jagged, so iterative procedures that only move downhill almost invariably get stuck far from a solution, random modifications help only slowly, and no speed-up techniques work well across broad classes of systems; hence natural systems are unlikely to come close to satisfying such constraints.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So what this suggests is that even if in some idealized sense a system in nature might be expected to satisfy certain constraints, it is likely that in practice the system will actually not have a way to come even close to doing this.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 7, “Mechanisms in Programs and Nature”; section “The Problem of Satisfying Constraints” (from p. 342), p. 348. Scope: iterative and annealing-like procedures for discrete constraint satisfaction, and natural systems assumed to satisfy constraints

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch07-17: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Algorithmic trapping is measurable on public benchmarks and simulations. Such tests discriminate the performance claims for defined instance families. They cannot establish impossibility across broad classes or the final generalization about how closely natural systems satisfy constraints.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Benchmark greedy descent, randomized local search, annealing, and modern solvers over preregistered ensembles of discrete constraint problems, measuring local-minimum trapping, residual violations, and scaling. Broadly persistent trapping and absence of a cross-class speedup would support the computational portion; efficient broad solvers or smooth landscapes would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Failure of tested algorithms cannot prove that no general speed-up works.

Almost always and broad classes depend on the benchmark distribution.

The inference to natural systems needs independent mechanistic data.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Jagged landscapes and trapping of downhill search are directly measurable on public constraint benchmarks, and those experiments are routine. A claim that no acceleration works across broad classes cannot be closed by any finite comparison, and the step from that fact to natural systems is an analogy rather than a dataset. The computational core is testable; the full conclusion is not settled by it.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On a broad sample of discrete constraint problems, run strict downhill search, neutral-or-downhill search, and standard accelerated heuristics, and record residual violation and time to a solution. Near-universal trapping of downhill search, with only slow gains from added randomness and no heuristic that succeeds across the sample, would support the computational half; a general method that reliably reaches solutions would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No speed-up works across broad classes is a negative existential and cannot be exhausted by the heuristics tried.

The inference from solver behavior to natural systems adds a step the benchmarks do not contain.
